label: thm:var
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:var}
	There exist absolute constants $C<\infty$ and $n_0$ such that for all $n\geqslant n_0$ and all $m\geqslant1$,
	\[
		\operatorname{Var}(S_{n,m})\leqslant C\bigl(\log^2\log n+{m}/{\log n}\bigr).
	\]

label: prop:fixedn
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:fixedn}
	For each fixed integer $n\geqslant2$, as $m\to\infty$,
	\[
		\frac{S_{n,m}-m}{\sqrt m}\implies\mathcal B_n:=
		\int_0^1\frac1u\,{\max_{1\leqslant i\leqslant n}(B_i(u)-\overline B(u))}\,du,
		\quad \overline B=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n B_i,
	\]
	where $B_1,B_{2},\ldots,B_n$ are independent standard Brownian bridges.
	The integral exists in $L^2$.
	The first moments also converge, with
	\[
		\frac{\operatorname{\mathds{E}} T_{n,m}-m}{\sqrt m}\longrightarrow\operatorname{\mathds{E}}\mathcal B_n=\frac\pi2 \operatorname{\mathds{E}}\max_{i\leqslant n}Z_i,
	\]
	where $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ are independent standard normal variables.

title: Remark
body_md:
For $n=2$, the known score limit~\cite{KP23} is
	\[
		\frac{T_{2,m}-m}{\sqrt m}\implies R,
		\quad\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(R\leqslant x)=1-e^{-x^2},\quad x\geqslant0.
	\]
	For fixed $n\geqslant3$, the score limit and its joint law with the compensator remain to be identified.

\label{prop:exp}
	Fix an integer $j\geqslant 2$. For $m\geqslant j$, let $\kappa_{m,j}:=(m)_j/m^j\in[j!/j^j,1]$. Then, as $n\to \infty$,

label: prop:capacitycoupling
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:capacitycoupling}
	Fix $n\geqslant1$. The reversed urn processes for all integer capacities $c\geqslant1$ can be coupled so that, almost surely, for every $c\leqslant d$ and every $0\leqslant t\leqslant nc$,
	\[
		\sum_{i=1}^k H_i^{(c)}(t)\leqslant\sum_{i=1}^k H_i^{(d)}(t),\quad1\leqslant k\leqslant n,
	\]
	where $H^{(c)}(t)$ is the height vector arranged in decreasing order.
	The total sums are both $t$. Thus $H^{(c)}(t)$ is majorized by $H^{(d)}(t)$. Under this coupling,
	\[
		W_t^{(c)}\leqslant W_t^{(d)}\text{ for }0\leqslant t\leqslant nc,\quad
		\tau_j^{(d)}\leqslant\tau_j^{(c)}\text{ for }1\leqslant j\leqslant c,\quad
		S_{n,c}\leqslant S_{n,d}.
	\]

label: lem:meanintegral
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Conditionally on $S_n(p)=\sum_{i=1}^nY_i(p)=t$, the count vector is multivariate hypergeometric with capacities $m$, hence its maximum has the law of $W_t$.
	Also $S_n(p)\sim\operatorname{Bin}(N,p)$, with $N=nm$. Since $W_0=0$, Tonelli's theorem and the beta integral give
	\[
		\int_0^1\frac{\operatorname{\mathds{E}} Z(p)}p\,dp
		=\sum_{t=1}^N\operatorname{\mathds{E}} W_t \ \binom Nt
		\int_0^1p^{t-1}(1-p)^{N-t}\,dp
		=\sum_{t=1}^N\frac{\operatorname{\mathds{E}} W_t}{t}=\operatorname{\mathds{E}} S_{n,m}.
	\]
	The equality $\operatorname{\mathds{E}} T_{n,m}=\operatorname{\mathds{E}} S_{n,m}$ and $\int_0^1mp\,dp/p=m$ finish the proof.
	Thus independence in~\eqref{eq:meanintegral} is exact after integration.
head: environment

label: lem:earlymean
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $f_j(\lambda)=\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(\operatorname{Bin}(m,\lambda/m)\geqslant j)$. Independence gives
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{E}} Z(\lambda/m)=\sum_{j=1}^m(1-(1-f_j(\lambda))^n).
	\]
	For $0\leqslant\lambda\leqslant j/2$, the single mass at $j$, the inequality
	$\binom mj\geqslant(m/j)^j$, and $\log(1-x)\geqslant-2x$ for $0\leqslant x\leqslant1/2$ give
	\[
		f_j(\lambda)\geqslant\binom mj(\lambda/m)^j(1-\lambda/m)^{m-j}
		\geqslant(\lambda/j)^j e^{-2\lambda}\geqslant(\lambda/(ej))^j.
	\]
	Therefore, for every integer $1\leqslant j\leqslant a$,
	\begin{align*}
		\int_0^a\{1-(1-f_j(\lambda))^n\}\frac{d\lambda}{\lambda}
		 & \geqslant\int_0^{j/2}\{1-e^{-n(\lambda/(ej))^j}\}\frac{d\lambda}{\lambda} \\
		 & =\frac1j\int_0^{n(2e)^{-j}}\frac{1-e^{-u}}u\,du
		\geqslant\frac{\log n}{j}-\log(2e)-\frac Cj.
	\end{align*}
	We used $\int_0^z(1-e^{-u})du/u\geqslant\log z-C$ for $z>0$.
	To see this,
	for $z\leqslant1$ the right side can be taken nonpositive, and for $z\geqslant1$ split the integral at one.
	Summing to $m$ when $m\leqslant \log n$, or to $\lfloor \log n\rfloor$ when $m\geqslant \log n$, gives the required lower bounds.

	For the upper bounds, the factorial-moment inequality gives
	$f_j(\lambda)\leqslant\binom mj(\lambda/m)^j\leqslant(e\lambda/j)^j$.
	Thus the integrand at level $j$ is at most $\min\{1,n(e\lambda/j)^j\}$.
	If $r_j=(j/e)n^{-1/j}$, direct integration gives
	\[
		\int_0^a\min\{1,(\lambda/r_j)^j\}\frac{d\lambda}{\lambda}
		\leqslant\left(\frac{\log n}{j}+\log\frac{ea}{j}\right)_++\frac1j
	\]
    where $x_+:=\max \{x,0\}$.
    
	For $m\leqslant \log n$, $r_j<m$ for $j\leqslant m$, and summing the exact expression gives
	\[
		I_{n,m}\leqslant (\log n)\mathcal{H}_m+\sum_{j=1}^m\log(em/j)+\mathcal{H}_m
		=(\log n)\mathcal{H}_m+O(m),
	\]
	using $\log(m!)\geqslant m\log m-m$.
	For $m\geqslant \log n$, sum the displayed upper bound first over $j\leqslant A\log n$, with a fixed $A>e^3$.
	The sum of $\log n/j$ is $(\log n)\log\log n+O(\log n)$, and
	$\sum_{j\geqslant1}(\log(e\log n/j))_+=O(\log n)$.
	For $j>A\log n$, the exact integral is $n(e\log n/j)^j/j\leqslant e^{-j}/j$.
	Summing this tail proves $I_{n,m}\leqslant (\log n)\log\log n+O(\log n)$.

label: lem:bulkmean
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $q=mp(1-p)$. The centered binomial satisfies the Bernstein moment-generating-function bound~\cite[Chapter 2]{BLM13}
	\[
		\log\operatorname{\mathds{E}} e^{t(Y_i(p)-mp)}\leqslant\frac{qt^2}{2(1-t/3)},\quad0<t<3.
	\]

	For $0<t<3$, Jensen's inequality gives
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{E}} Z(p)-mp\leqslant\frac{\log n}{t}+\frac{qt}{2(1-t/3)}.
	\]
	When $q>0$, take
	$t=\sqrt{2\log n/q}/\{1+\sqrt{2\log n/q}/3\}$.
	When $q=0$, the maximum is deterministic.
	Thus

	\begin{align}\label{eq:binmaxupper}
		0\leqslant\operatorname{\mathds{E}} Z(p)-mp\leqslant\sqrt{2q\log n}+\log n/3.
	\end{align}
	Consequently, with $r=m/\log n\geqslant1$,
	\[
		J_{n,m}\leqslant\sqrt{2m\log n}\int_{\log n/m}^1\sqrt{\frac{1-p}{p}}\,dp
		+\frac{\log n}{3}\log r.
	\]
	This proves the bounded-$r$ assertion.
	If $r\to\infty$, then
	$(\log n)\log r=o(\sqrt{m\log n})$ and the integral tends to $\pi/2$, proving the upper half of~\eqref{eq:bulkmean}.

	For the matching lower bound, fix $\delta\in(0,1/2)$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$.
	Uniformly for $p\in[\delta,1-\delta]$, define
	$d:=(1-\varepsilon)\sqrt{2q\log n}$ and $k=\lceil mp+d\rceil$.
	Since $\log n=o(m)$, $d=o(m)$ and the integer block
	$k\leqslant\ell\leqslant k+\lfloor\sqrt{q/\log n}\rfloor$ lies in the binomial support for all sufficiently large $n$.
	Stirling's bounds give, uniformly in this block,
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(Y_i(p)=\ell)\geqslant\frac{c_\delta}{\sqrt q}
		\exp(-m D(\ell/m\Vert p)-C_\delta),
	\]
	where $D(x\Vert p)=x\log(x/p)+(1-x)\log((1-x)/(1-p))$.
	Taylor expansion on the compact interval gives
	\[
		mD(\ell/m\Vert p)=(1-\varepsilon)^2\log n+o(\log n).
	\]
	This holds uniformly in $p$ and $\ell$.
	The cubic remainder is $O_\delta((\log n)\sqrt{\log n/m})=o(\log n)$.
	Rounding and the block width contribute $O_\delta(1)+o(1)$ to the quadratic term.
	Summing the block, whose length is of order $\sqrt{q/\log n}$, yields
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(Y_i(p)\geqslant mp+d)
		\geqslant\frac{c_\delta}{\sqrt{\log n}}\exp\{-(1-\varepsilon)^2\log n-o(\log n)\}.
	\]
	Its product with $n$ tends to infinity uniformly in $p$.
	Independence therefore implies $\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(Z(p)\geqslant mp+d)=1-o(1)$ uniformly.
	Moreover, $\operatorname{\mathds{E}}(mp-Z(p))_+\leqslant\operatorname{\mathds{E}}|Y_1(p)-mp|\leqslant\sqrt q$, so
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{E}} Z(p)-mp\geqslant(1-\varepsilon)\sqrt{2q\log n}(1-o(1))-\sqrt q.
	\]
	Integrating over $[\delta,1-\delta]$, which is contained in $[\log n/m,1]$ eventually, gives
	\[
		\liminf\frac{J_{n,m}}{\sqrt{m\log n}}
		\geqslant(1-\varepsilon)\sqrt2\int_\delta^{1-\delta}\sqrt{\frac{1-p}{p}}\,dp.
	\]
	Letting $\varepsilon,\delta\downarrow0$ proves the lower half.

head: environment

label: prob_conv_1
title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that $\mu_{n,m}:=\operatorname{\mathds{E}} S_{n,m}$ and
	\begin{align*}
		V_N := \sum_{k=1}^{N}\operatorname{\mathds{E}}( (M_{k}-M_{k-1})^2\mid \mathcal{F}_{k-1}) =\sum_{k=1}^{N} \pi_{k-1}^* (1 - \pi_{k-1}^*) = S_{n,m} - \sum_{k=1}^{N} \left\vert\pi_{k-1}^*\right\vert^2.
	\end{align*}
	By Lemmas~\ref{lem:easylb} and~\ref{lem:pisquared}, we know that $\mu_{n,m}\to\infty$ and $\operatorname{\mathds{E}}(\left\vertV_N-S_{n,m}\right\vert)/\mu_{n,m}\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$.
	Now,
	\begin{align*}
		\operatorname{\mathds{E}}(\left\vertV_N/\mu_{n,m}-1\right\vert)
		\leqslant \frac{1}{\mu_{n,m}}\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(S_{n,m})} +\frac{1}{\mu_{n,m}}\operatorname{\mathds{E}}(\left\vertV_N-S_{n,m}\right\vert).
	\end{align*}
	Thus, under the condition that $\operatorname{Var}(S_{n,m})/\mu_{n,m}^2 \to 0$ as $n\to\infty$, we can say that
	\begin{align}\label{prob_conv_1}
		\lim_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{\mathds{E}}(\left\vertV_N/\mu_{n,m}-1\right\vert) = 0,
	\end{align}
	so that $V_N/\mu_{n,m}\to 1$ in probability.
	Since $|M_k-M_{k-1}|\leqslant1$ and $\mu_{n,m}\to\infty$, for each $\varepsilon>0$ the normalized conditional Lindeberg sum is exactly zero for all sufficiently large $n$:
	\[
		\frac1{\mu_{n,m}}\sum_{k=1}^N\operatorname{\mathds{E}}\left((M_k-M_{k-1})^2
		\mathds{1}_{\{|M_k-M_{k-1}|>\varepsilon\sqrt{\mu_{n,m}}\}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k-1}\right)=0.
	\]
	Let $\sigma_N^2=\operatorname{Var}(M_N)=\operatorname{\mathds{E}} V_N$.
	Lemma~\ref{lem:pisquared} gives $\sigma_N^2/\mu_{n,m}\to1$.
	Since $V_N/\sigma_N^2\to1$ in probability and the conditional Lindeberg condition holds, the martingale central limit theorem with deterministic limiting variance~\cite{HH80} gives $M_N/\sigma_N\implies\operatorname{N}(0,1)$. Slutsky's lemma completes the proof.

title: Remark
body_md:
If one uses the universal bound~\eqref{eq:varSuniv} instead of Theorem~\ref{thm:var}, the same argument gives
	\[
		\frac{\operatorname{Var}(S_{n,m})}{(\operatorname{\mathds{E}} S_{n,m})^2}\leqslant \frac{Cm}{(m-1+\mathcal{H}_n)^2}\leqslant \frac{C}{\mathcal{H}_n}\to 0,

label: lem:Bsquared
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:Bsquared}
	Define $B_N:=\sum_{k=1}^N\left\vert\pi_{k-1}^*\right\vert^2$.
	For all sufficiently large $n$ and every $m\geqslant1$,
	\begin{align}\label{eq:BL2}
		\|B_N\|_2\leqslant C\left(1+\frac mn\right).
	\end{align}
	In particular, if $\mu_{n,m}=\operatorname{\mathds{E}} S_{n,m}$, then
	\[
		\frac{\operatorname{\mathds{E}} B_N}{\mu_{n,m}}\leqslant C\left(\frac{1}{\mu_{n,m}}+\frac1n\right),\quad
		\frac{\operatorname{\mathds{E}} B_N^2}{\mu_{n,m}^2}\leqslant C\left(\frac1{\mu_{n,m}^2}+\frac1{n^2}\right).
	\]
head: environment
name: Squared success probabilities

title: Proof
body_md:
The multinomial comparison in Corollary~\ref{cor:capacitycomparisons} gives
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(W_t\geqslant k)\leqslant \min\left(1,n\left(\frac{et}{nk}\right)^k\right).
	\]
	We first prove two fourth-moment bounds.
	If $t\leqslant\sqrt n$ and $k\geqslant4$, then, for $n\geqslant4e^2$,
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(W_t\geqslant k)\leqslant n(e/\sqrt n)^k
		\leqslant\frac{e^4}{n}\,2^{-(k-4)}.
	\]
	The identity
	$\operatorname{\mathds{E}} W_t^4=\sum_{k\geqslant1}(k^4-(k-1)^4)\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(W_t\geqslant k)$
	therefore gives $\|W_t\|_4\leqslant C$ in this range.
	For any $t$, let $a_t=\lceil2et/n+4\log n\rceil$.
	For integers $k\geqslant a_t$, we have
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(W_t\geqslant k)\leqslant n2^{-k}
		\leqslant e^{-(\log2-1/4)k}.
	\]
	Summing the same moment identity gives
	$\|W_t\|_4\leqslant C(t/n+\log n)$.
	Now, we use time reversal and Minkowski's inequality.
	They give
	\begin{align*}
		\|B_N\|_2
	 \leqslant\sum_{t=1}^{nm}\frac{\|W_t\|_4^2}{t^2}                        
		 & \leqslant C\sum_{t\leqslant\sqrt n}\frac1{t^2}
		+C\sum_{\sqrt n<t\leqslant nm}\left(\frac1{n^2}+\frac{(\log n)^2}{t^2}\right) \\
		 & \leqslant C\left(1+\frac mn+\frac{(\log n)^2}{\sqrt n}\right)
		\leqslant C\left(1+\frac mn\right).
	\end{align*}
	Since $\mu_{n,m}\geqslant m$, division by $\mu_{n,m}$ proves the remaining assertions.
	No independence between different times is used.

label: eq:Bernmoments
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $S=S_{n,m}$, $M=T_{n,m}-S$, $\mu=\operatorname{\mathds{E}} S$ and $v=\operatorname{Var} S$.
	Let $D_k=\operatorname{\mathbf{score}}_k-\pi_{k-1}^*$ and abbreviate $p_k=\pi_{k-1}^*$.
	The conditional Bernoulli law gives, for every $r\geqslant2$,
	\begin{align}\label{eq:Bernmoments}
		\operatorname{\mathds{E}}(|D_k|^r\mid\mathcal{F}_{k-1})
		 & =p_k(1-p_k)((1-p_k)^{r-1}+p_k^{r-1})
		  \leqslant p_k(1-p_k)
		=\operatorname{\mathds{E}}(D_k^2\mid\mathcal{F}_{k-1}).\notag
	\end{align}
	In particular, $\xi_k=D_k/\sqrt\mu$ satisfies
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{E}}(|\xi_k|^3\mid\mathcal{F}_{k-1})
		\leqslant\mu^{-1/2}\operatorname{\mathds{E}}(\xi_k^2\mid\mathcal{F}_{k-1}),\quad
		\max_k|\xi_k|\leqslant\mu^{-1/2}.
	\]
	For large $n$, $\mu^{-1/2}\leqslant1/2$ uniformly in $m$.
	Thus condition (A1) of Fan~\cite{Fan19} holds with $\rho=1$ and $\epsilon=\mu^{-1/2}$.
	The normalized predictable quadratic variation is
	\[
		Q=\sum_k\operatorname{\mathds{E}}(\xi_k^2\mid\mathcal{F}_{k-1})=\frac{S-B_N}{\mu}.
	\]
	Lemma~\ref{lem:Bsquared} gives
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{E}}|Q-1|^2\leqslant\frac{2v+2\operatorname{\mathds{E}} B_N^2}{\mu^2}
		\leqslant C\left(\frac{v+1}{\mu^2}+\frac1{n^2}\right).
	\]
	Fan's Theorem 2.2, with moment parameter $p=2$, gives
	\[
		d_K(M/\sqrt\mu,\operatorname{N}(0,1))
		\leqslant C\left(\epsilon|\log\epsilon|
		+\left(\operatorname{\mathds{E}}|Q-1|^2+\operatorname{\mathds{E}}\max_k|\xi_k|^4\right)^{1/5}\right).
	\]
	Since $\operatorname{\mathds{E}}\max_k|\xi_k|^4\leqslant\mu^{-2}$, we obtain
	\[
		d_K(M/\sqrt\mu,\operatorname{N}(0,1))
		\leqslant C\left(\frac{\log(2+\mu)}{\sqrt\mu}
		+\left(\frac{v+1}{\mu^2}+\frac1{n^2}\right)^{1/5}\right).
	\]

	For the score, first use normalization by $\sqrt\mu$.
	Define $Z:=M/\sqrt\mu$ and $U=(S-\mu)/\sqrt\mu$.
	For every $\delta>0$,
	\begin{align*}
		\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(Z\leqslant x-\delta)-\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(|U|>\delta)
		 & \leqslant\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(Z+U\leqslant x)                       
		 \leqslant\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(Z\leqslant x+\delta)+\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(|U|>\delta).
	\end{align*}
	The bounded normal density and Chebyshev's inequality imply
	\[
		d_K((T_{n,m}-\mu)/\sqrt\mu,\operatorname{N}(0,1))
		\leqslant d_K(Z,\operatorname{N}(0,1))+C\delta+\frac{v}{\mu\delta^2}.
	\]
	Take $\delta=(v/\mu)^{1/3}$ if $v>0$.
	If $v=0$, then $U=0$ almost surely.
	This proves the asserted bound with normalization by $\sqrt\mu$.

	To replace $\sqrt\mu$ by $\sigma:=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(T_{n,m})}$, define $\sigma_M^2:=\operatorname{Var} M=\mu-\operatorname{\mathds{E}} B_N$.
	The reverse triangle inequality gives $|\sigma-\sigma_M|\leqslant\sqrt v$.
	Consequently,
	\[
		\left|\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt\mu}-1\right|
		\leqslant C\left(\sqrt{\frac v\mu}+\frac1\mu+\frac1n\right).
	\]
	Here $\sigma_M^2\geqslant\mu/2$ for large $n$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:Bsquared}.
	Theorem~\ref{thm:var} also gives $v/\mu\to0$ uniformly.
	Normal scale comparison costs at most the last displayed bound.
	For $0\leqslant v/\mu\leqslant1$, its square-root term is at most $(v/\mu)^{1/3}$.
	The other terms are absorbed by $\{(v+1)/\mu^2+n^{-2}\}^{1/5}$.
	Thus the score bound follows without any independence assumption on $M$ and $S$.
	Finally, Theorem~\ref{thm:var} and $\mu\geqslant\max(m,\mathcal{H}_n)$ imply
	\[
		\frac{v+1}{\mu^2}
		\leqslant C\frac{(1+\log\log n)^2}{(\log n)^2},\quad
		\frac v\mu\leqslant C\frac{(1+\log\log n)^2}{\log n}.
	\]
	For the first inequality, use $m/\mu^2\leqslant1/\mu\leqslant1/\log n$.
	Also $\log(2+\mu)/\sqrt\mu\leqslant C\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n}$ for large $n$.
	Both terms in the martingale estimate are $o((1+\log\log n)^{2/3}/(\log n)^{1/3})$, uniformly in $m$.
	This proves~\eqref{eq:uniformrate}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Take a single sequence of independent $U_t\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$, $t\geqslant1$.
	For every capacity $c$, start all bins at zero.
	At time $t<nc$, sort the bins by decreasing current height, retaining their labels and breaking height ties by increasing label.
	If their sorted heights are $h_1\geqslant\cdots\geqslant h_n$, set
	\[
		F_c(h;r)=\frac{rc-\sum_{i=1}^r h_i}{nc-t},\quad 0\leqslant r\leqslant n,
	\]
	with $F_c(h;0)=0$. Increment the bin of rank
	\[
		I_c(t+1)=\min\{r\in[n]:U_{t+1}\leqslant F_c(h;r)\},
	\]
	and sort again.
	Each bin of height $h_i$ is chosen with probability
	$(c-h_i)/(nc-t)$, so retaining labels gives exactly the required urn-process marginal.

	We show that one common-uniform step preserves majorization for arbitrary capacities $c\leqslant d$.
	Suppose the sorted states $x,y$ at time $t<nc$ satisfy $x\preceq_{\mathrm{maj}}y$.
	Write $X_k=\sum_{i\leqslant k}x_i$ and $Y_k=\sum_{i\leqslant k}y_i$.
	After one increment and reordering, every partial sum increases by either zero or one.
	Thus, because the heights are integers, only a tight partial sum $X_k=Y_k$ could violate the order.

	Fix such a $k<n$, and put
	$r_x=\max\{i:x_i=x_k\}$ and $r_y=\max\{i:y_i=y_k\}$.
	The top-$k$ sum increases precisely when the selected rank is at most $r_x$ or $r_y$, respectively.
	We claim that $r_x\leqslant r_y$ and $X_{r_x}=Y_{r_x}$.
	If $r_x=k$, these assertions follow immediately from tightness and $r_y\geqslant k$.
	If $r_x>k$, then $x_{k+1}=x_k$.
	Tightness at $k$ and majorization at $k-1$ imply $x_k\geqslant y_k$.
	Majorization at $k+1$ gives
	$x_k=x_{k+1}\leqslant y_{k+1}\leqslant y_k\leqslant x_k$.
	Hence all these heights are equal, and the same argument propagates through the tie block of $x$ up to $r_x$.
	This proves the claim.
	The case $k=n$ needs no comparison, since both totals increase by one.

	Define $r=r_x$ and $H=X_r=Y_r$. Since $x$ is decreasing, $nH\geqslant rt$.
	For $a>t/n$, direct differentiation gives
	\[
		\frac{d}{da}\left(\frac{ra-H}{na-t}\right)
		=\frac{nH-rt}{(na-t)^2}\geqslant0.
	\]
	Consequently,
	\[
		F_c(x;r_x)\leqslant F_d(y;r_x)\leqslant F_d(y;r_y).
	\]
	Under the common uniform coupling, whenever the tight top-$k$ sum of $x$ increases, the corresponding sum of $y$ also increases.
	Every partial-sum inequality therefore survives the step.
	Starting from equal zero vectors proves the claimed order at all common times.
	Since the same uniforms serve every capacity, the construction is simultaneous for all integer capacities, and the almost-sure assertion holds for their countably many pairs and times.
	Taking $k=1$ gives the maximum comparison.
	Evaluating it at the smaller-capacity hitting time gives the hitting-time comparison.
	Finally, the backward representation~\eqref{eq:SW}, the maximum comparison on $t\leqslant nc$, and the positive extra terms on $nc<t\leqslant nd$ give the compensator comparison.

name: Conditional binomials and multinomial comparison

title: Proof
body_md:
Conditioning independent binomials on their sum gives the mass function
	$\prod_i\binom m{x_i}/\binom{nm}t$, identical to the urn occupancy law.
	The first assertion follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:capacitycoupling}.
	For fixed $n,t$, the occupancy mass function at capacity $d$ can be written
	\[
		\frac{t!}{\prod_i x_i!}\frac{\prod_i(d)_{x_i}}{(nd)_t}
		\longrightarrow\frac{t!}{\prod_i x_i!}n^{-t}\text{ as }d\to\infty,
	\]
	where $\sum_i x_i=t$. The finite support and the capacity comparison prove~\eqref{eq:multcomparison}.
	Finally, each $Z_i(t)$ is $\operatorname{Bin}(t,1/n)$, so
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(Z_i(t)\geqslant k)\leqslant\operatorname{\mathds{E}}\binom{Z_i(t)}k
		=\binom tk n^{-k}\leqslant\left(\frac{et}{nk}\right)^k.
	\]
	The union bound proves~\eqref{eq:multmaxbound}.
	For $k>t$, the probability is zero.

label: lem:hyp
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:hyp}
	Fix $1\leqslant j\leqslant m$.
	\begin{enumeratea}
		\item\label{hyp:a} For all $0\leqslant t\leqslant N$,
		\[
			\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(W_t\geqslant j)\leqslant n\,p_j(t)\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{\mathds{P}}(W_t\leqslant j-1)\leqslant \bigl(1-p_j(t)\bigr)^n\leqslant e^{-n p_j(t)}.
		\]
		\item\label{hyp:b} For all $0\leqslant t\leqslant N-1$,
		\[
			p_j(t+1)-p_j(t)=\frac{j}{t+1}\,h_{t+1}(j).
		\]
		\item\label{hyp:c} For all $j\leqslant s\leqslant nj$,
		\[
			h_s(j)\geqslant \frac{1}{e^2\sqrt{j}}\; p_j(s).
		\]
	\end{enumeratea}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\ref{hyp:a} The first inequality is the union bound.
	For the second, use negative association of the multivariate hypergeometric vector.
	See Joag-Dev and Proschan~\cite[Section 3.1]{JDP83}.
	Negative association applies also to decreasing functions on disjoint coordinate sets.
	Iterating it for the indicators $\mathds{1}{\{\widetilde X_i(t)\leqslant x_i\}}$ gives

	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{P}}\bigl(\widetilde X_i(t)\leqslant x_i\ \forall i\in[n]\bigr)\leqslant \prod_{i=1}^n \operatorname{\mathds{P}}\bigl(\widetilde X_i(t)\leqslant x_i\bigr).
	\] Taking $x_i=j-1$ for all $i$ gives $\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(W_t\leqslant j-1)\leqslant (1-p_j(t))^n$, and $1-x\leqslant e^{-x}$ finishes the proof.

	\ref{hyp:b} Let $\xi_{t+1}$ be the indicator that the $(t+1)$-th ball goes into urn $1$. Then
	\[
		\{\widetilde X_1(t+1)\geqslant j\}\setminus\{\widetilde X_1(t)\geqslant j\}=\{\widetilde X_1(t+1)=j,\ \xi_{t+1}=1\}.
	\]
	If $h_{t+1}(j)=0$, both sides vanish. Otherwise, condition on $\widetilde X_1(t+1)=j$.
	The $j$ type-1 positions are exchangeable among these $t+1$ cards.
	Thus the final ball belongs to urn 1 with probability $j/(t+1)$. Hence $p_j(t+1)-p_j(t)=\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(\widetilde X_1(t+1)=j)\cdot j/(t+1)$.

	\ref{hyp:c} Fix $s$ with $j\leqslant s\leqslant nj$. For $k\geqslant j$ with $h_s(k)>0$, that is, $j\leqslant k\leqslant \min(m,s)$, we have from~\eqref{eq:hyppmf}
	\begin{align}\label{eq:ratio}
		r_k(s):=\frac{h_s(k+1)}{h_s(k)}=\frac{(m-k)(s-k)}{(k+1)(N-m-s+k+1)},
	\end{align}
	where the denominator is positive because $s\leqslant nj$ and $k\geqslant j$ give $N-m-s+k+1\geqslant (n-1)(m-j)+1\geqslant 1$. (When $k=\min(m,s)$ the formula correctly gives $r_k(s)=0$.) We make two observations.
	First, $r_j(s)$ is nondecreasing in $s$, and at $s=nj$
	\[
		r_j(nj)=\frac{(m-j)\,j(n-1)}{(j+1)\bigl((n-1)(m-j)+1\bigr)}<1,
	\]
	so that $r_j(s)\leqslant 1$ for all $s\leqslant nj$. Second, for $j\leqslant k<\min(m,s)$, comparing the four factors in~\eqref{eq:ratio} at $k$ and $k+1$,
	\[
		\frac{r_{k+1}(s)}{r_k(s)}=\frac{m-k-1}{m-k}\cdot\frac{s-k-1}{s-k}\cdot\frac{k+1}{k+2}\cdot\frac{N-m-s+k+1}{N-m-s+k+2}\leqslant \frac{k+1}{k+2}.
	\]
	Iterating, $r_l(s)\leqslant r_j(s)\,\frac{j+1}{l+1}\leqslant \frac{j+1}{l+1}$ for all $j\leqslant l\leqslant \min(m,s)$ (the bound is trivial once $r_l(s)=0$). Therefore, for every $0\leqslant i\leqslant \min(m,s)-j$,
	\[
		h_s(j+i)=h_s(j)\prod_{l=j}^{j+i-1} r_l(s)\leqslant h_s(j)\prod_{l=j}^{j+i-1}\frac{j+1}{l+1}=h_s(j)\,\frac{(j+1)^i\, j!}{(j+i)!}.
	\]
    For $i>\min(m,s)-j$, $h_s(j+i)=0$, so the same upper bound holds. Summing over $i\geqslant 0$ and using $j!\leqslant e\sqrt{j}\,(j/e)^j$,
	\begin{align*}
		p_j(s) & \leqslant h_s(j)\, j!\,(j+1)^{-j}\sum_{i\geqslant 0}\frac{(j+1)^{j+i}}{(j+i)!} \\
		       & \leqslant h_s(j)\, j!\,(j+1)^{-j}e^{j+1}
		\leqslant h_s(j)\, e^2\sqrt{j}\,\bigl(\frac{j}{j+1}\bigr)^{j}\leqslant e^2\sqrt{j}\,h_s(j).
	\end{align*}
	This completes the proof.

label: lem:tailwindow
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:tailwindow}
	Let $U$ take values in $\{1,2,\ldots,R\}$, and let $g$ be nondecreasing on $\{0,1,\ldots,R\}$ with
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(U\leqslant t)\leqslant g(t),\quad \operatorname{\mathds{P}}(U>t)\leqslant e^{-g(t)}.
	\]
	Suppose $h:=\min\{t:g(t)\geqslant1\}$ exists, and for integers $0\leqslant t\leqslant t'\leqslant E$, with $h\leqslant E\leqslant R$,
	\[
		g(t)\leqslant g(t')\left(\frac{t+1}{t'+1}\right)^\beta,
		\quad 0<\beta\leqslant2h.
	\]
	If $E=R$, then $\operatorname{\mathds{E}}\log^2(U/h)\leqslant C/\beta^2$.
	If $E<R$, assume additionally that, for $0\leqslant t\leqslant t'\leqslant R$,
	\[
		g(t)\leqslant g(t')\left(\frac{t+1}{t'+1}\right)^\alpha,
		\quad 0<\alpha\leqslant E,
	\]
	and define $x_*:=\log(E/h)$. If $\beta x_*\geqslant6$ and $K:=e^{\beta x_*/2}$, then
	\begin{align}\label{eq:windowbound}
		\operatorname{\mathds{E}}\log^2(U/h)\leqslant
		C\left(\beta^{-2}+\alpha^{-2}e^{-K}
		 +(\alpha\beta)^{-1}e^{-K/2}\right).
	\end{align}
head: environment
name: Concentration from discrete elasticity

title: Proof
body_md:
For the lower tail, take $t=\lfloor he^{-x}\rfloor$. If $t=0$, then $U\geqslant1>he^{-x}$ and the probability is zero.
	Otherwise $t\leqslant h-1$ and $g(h-1)<1$, so
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(\log(U/h)<-x)\leqslant e^{-\beta x}(1+e^x/h)^\beta.
	\]
	For $0<x\leqslant2\log2$ the final factor is at most $e^8$, because $\beta/h\leqslant2$. For $x\geqslant2\log2$, whenever $t\geqslant1$ it is at most $2^\beta\leqslant e^{\beta x/2}$. Integrating $2x$ times these bounds gives $C/\beta^2$.
	For the upper tail, $t=\lfloor he^x\rfloor\leqslant E$ implies
	\[
		g(t)\geqslant g(h)\left(\frac{t+1}{h+1}\right)^\beta
		\geqslant e^{-2}e^{\beta x},
	\]
	where the equality-endpoint case is included.
	Thus the integral of $2x\exp(-e^{-2}e^{\beta x})$ is $C/\beta^2$. If $E=R$, the remaining upper tail is zero, proving the first claim.
	Otherwise $g(E)\geqslant e^{-2}e^{\beta x_*}$. For $x>x_*$ and $t<R$, the weaker elasticity and $\alpha/E\leqslant1$ give
	\[
		g(t)\geqslant g(E)e^{-1}e^{\alpha(x-x_*)}
		\geqslant K e^{\alpha(x-x_*)}.
	\]
	For $t\geqslant R$, the upper-tail probability is zero.
	Writing $y=x-x_*$ and using $e^{\alpha y}\geqslant1+\alpha y$, the remaining integral is at most
	\[
		e^{-K}\left(\frac{2}{K^2\alpha^2}+\frac{2x_*}{K\alpha}\right).
	\]
	With $u=\beta x_*/2$ we have
	$x_*e^{-K/2}=(2/\beta)u e^{-e^u/2}\leqslant C/\beta$.
	This proves~\eqref{eq:windowbound}.

label: eq:tails
title: Proof
body_md:
Define $g(t)=np_j(t)$ and define $t_j=\min\{t:g(t)\geqslant1\}$. Since $g(t)=0$ for $t<j$ and $g(nj)\geqslant\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(W_{nj}\geqslant j)=1$, we have $j\leqslant t_j\leqslant nj$. Lemma~\ref{lem:hyp}\ref{hyp:a} gives
	\begin{align}\label{eq:tails}
		\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(\tau_j\leqslant t)\leqslant g(t),\quad \operatorname{\mathds{P}}(\tau_j>t)\leqslant e^{-g(t)}.
	\end{align}
	Apply the full-window case of Lemma~\ref{lem:tailwindow} with $U=\tau_j$, $h=t_j$, $E=R=nj$ and $\beta=\sqrt j/e^2$. The required elasticity is~\eqref{eq:elast}.
	The equal-endpoint case is an equality.
	Since $\beta\leqslant t_j$, the result follows with an absolute constant $C_0$.

label: eq:Hlog
title: Proof
body_md:
We first note the elementary inequality
	\begin{align}\label{eq:Hlog}
		\left\vert\mathcal{H}_{a-1}-\mathcal{H}_{b-1}\right\vert\leqslant 2\left\vert\log(a/b)\right\vert\quad\text{for all integers } a,b\geqslant 1.
	\end{align}
	Indeed, for $a>b$,
	\[
		\mathcal{H}_{a-1}-\mathcal{H}_{b-1}=\sum_{k=b+1}^{a}\frac1k+\frac1b-\frac1a\leqslant \int_b^a\frac{dx}{x}+\frac{a-b}{ab}\leqslant \log\frac ab+\biggl(1-\frac ba\biggr)\leqslant 2\log\frac ab,
	\]
	using $1-y\leqslant -\log y$ for $y\in(0,1]$.
	Let $t_j$ be as in Proposition~\ref{prop:logTj}.
	By~\eqref{eq:Hlog} and Proposition~\ref{prop:logTj},
	\[
		\operatorname{Var}(\mathcal{H}_{\tau_j-1})\leqslant \operatorname{\mathds{E}}\bigl((\mathcal{H}_{\tau_j-1}-\mathcal{H}_{t_j-1})^2\bigr)\leqslant 4\,\operatorname{\mathds{E}}\bigl(\log^2(\tau_j/t_j)\bigr)\leqslant \frac{4C_0}{j}.
	\]
	By the representation~\eqref{eq:STj} and Minkowski's inequality,
	\[
		\left\VertS_{n,m}-\operatorname{\mathds{E}} S_{n,m}\right\Vert_2=\bigl\lVert\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(\mathcal{H}_{\tau_j-1}-\operatorname{\mathds{E}}(\mathcal{H}_{\tau_j-1})\bigr)\bigr\rVert_2\leqslant \sum_{j=1}^m \sqrt{\frac{4C_0}{j}}\leqslant 4\sqrt{C_0\, m}.
	\]
	Hence $\operatorname{Var}(S_{n,m})\leqslant 16 C_0\, m$, which is~\eqref{eq:varSuniv} with $C=16C_0$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:tjloc}
	Let $\rho_0:=e^{-1/(2\lambda)}$. There exists $n_0=n_0(\lambda)$ such that for all $n\geqslant n_0$, all $m\geqslant1$ and all $1\leqslant j\leqslant \min(m,\lambda\log n)$, the hitting scale $t_j$ defined in Proposition~\ref{prop:logTj} satisfies
	\[

head: environment
name: Location of $t_j$

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $t_0=\lfloor\rho_0nj\rfloor$, define $A=4e^2$ and define
	\[
		a_j=\rho_0e^{-A/\sqrt j},\quad u_j=\lfloor a_jnj\rfloor.
	\]
	For $n$ sufficiently large depending only on $\lambda$, $j\leqslant u_j<t_0$ uniformly in $1\leqslant j\leqslant\lambda\log n$.
	Consider first the process with capacity exactly $j$. A given bin is full at time $u_j$ with probability
	\[
		p_j^{(j)}(u_j)=\frac{(u_j)_j}{(nj)_j}
		\geqslant(a_j-1/n)^j\geqslant\tfrac12 a_j^j.
	\]
	The last inequality holds uniformly because $a_j\geqslant\rho_0e^{-A}>0$ and $j=O_\lambda(\log n)$.
	Since $\rho_0^j\geqslant n^{-1/2}$,
	\[
		np_j^{(j)}(u_j)\geqslant\tfrac12\sqrt n\,
		\exp\{-A\sqrt{\lambda\log n}\}\longrightarrow\infty
	\]
	uniformly in $j$.
	Negative association gives
	$\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(W_{u_j}^{(j)}<j)\leqslant\exp\{-np_j^{(j)}(u_j)\}$.
	The capacity coupling therefore implies, for every $m\geqslant j$,
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(W_{u_j}^{(m)}\geqslant j)\geqslant\tfrac12,
		\quad np_j^{(m)}(u_j)\geqslant\tfrac12,
	\]
	where the second inequality is the union bound.
	Apply the universal elasticity~\eqref{eq:elast} between $u_j$ and $t_0$, with $\beta=\sqrt j/e^2$.
	The rounding error is $O_\lambda(1/n)$, uniformly in $j$.
	Since $j\leqslant\lambda\log n$, for sufficiently large $n$,
	\[
		\log\frac{t_0+1}{u_j+1}\geqslant\frac{A}{2\sqrt j}.
	\]
	Consequently,
	\[
		np_j^{(m)}(t_0)\geqslant\tfrac12
		\left(\frac{t_0+1}{u_j+1}\right)^\beta
		\geqslant\tfrac12e^{A/(2e^2)}>1.
	\]
	By the definition of $t_j$, this gives $t_j\leqslant t_0\leqslant\rho_0nj$.

head: environment
name: Elasticity of order $j$

title: Proof
body_md:
Lemma~\ref{lem:hyp}\ref{hyp:c} gives $r_l(s)\leqslant r_j(s)$ for $l\geqslant j$.
	Whenever $r_j(s)<1$, summing the geometric bound yields
	\[
		p_j(s)\leqslant\frac{h_s(j)}{1-r_j(s)},\quad \phi_j(s)\geqslant1-r_j(s).
	\]
	By~\eqref{eq:ratio}, $r_j(s)$ is nondecreasing in $s$.
	For $s\leqslant\rho_1nj$,
	\begin{align*}
		r_j(s)
		 & \leqslant \frac{(m-j)\,\rho_1 nj}{(j+1)\bigl(nm-m-\rho_1 nj\bigr)}               \\
		 & \leqslant \frac{(m-j)\,\rho_1 j}{(j+1)(m-\rho_1 j)}\cdot\frac{n}{n-1/(1-\rho_1)}
		\leqslant \rho_1\cdot\frac{n}{n-1/(1-\rho_1)}\leqslant \rho_2,
	\end{align*}
	where we used $m\leqslant (m-\rho_1 j)/(1-\rho_1)$, then $(m-j)/(m-\rho_1 j)\leqslant 1, j/(j+1)\leqslant1$, and finally $n\geqslant n_0(\lambda)\geqslant (1+\rho_1)/(1-\rho_1)^2$. This proves the first claim, and~\eqref{eq:elastj} follows exactly as~\eqref{eq:elast} was derived from Lemma~\ref{lem:hyp}\ref{hyp:b},\ref{hyp:c}, with $\alpha_j$ replaced by $j(1-\rho_2)$.

title: Proof

label: lem:stirling
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Applying~\eqref{eq:binomrobbins} to the three binomial coefficients in $h_t(k)=\binom mk\binom{N-m}{t-k}\big/\binom Nt$ (lower bounds for the two in the numerator, the upper bound for the denominator) gives
	\[
		h_t(k)\ \geqslant\ \frac29\sqrt{\frac{t(1-t/N)}{k(1-k/m)\,(t-k)\bigl(1-\frac{t-k}{N-m}\bigr)}}\;e^{-\Lambda_t(k)}.
	\]
	Here $t/(t-k)\geqslant1$, and with $t=n\mu$, $N=nm$,
	\[
		\frac{1-t/N}{1-\frac{t-k}{N-m}}=\frac{(N-t)(N-m)}{N\,(N-m-t+k)}=\frac{(n-1)(m-\mu)}{n(m-\mu)-(m-k)}\ \geqslant\ 1-\frac1n\ \geqslant\ \frac12,
	\]
	using $m-k\geqslant0$. Since $\frac{2}{9\sqrt2}>\frac17$, this proves~\eqref{eq:hstirling}.

	For the bounds on $\Lambda_t$, regard $\Lambda_t(x)$ as a function of a real variable $x\in(0,m)$ with $0<t-x<N-m$. It is smooth there, with
	\begin{align*}
	\Lambda_t'(x) &=\log\frac{x}{m-x}-\log\frac{t-x}{N-m-t+x},\\
		\Lambda_t''(x)&=\frac1x+\frac{1}{m-x}+\frac{1}{t-x}+\frac{1}{N-m-t+x}>0.
	\end{align*}
	At $x=\mu=t/n$ we have $\frac{t-\mu}{N-m-t+\mu}=\frac{(n-1)\mu}{(n-1)(m-\mu)}=\frac{\mu}{m-\mu}$, so $\Lambda_t'(\mu)=0$, and 
    $$
    \Lambda_t(\mu)=NH(\mu/m)-mH(\mu/m)-(N-m)H(\mu/m)=0.
    $$ 
    Hence, for $k\geqslant \mu,$
    we have
	\begin{align}\label{eq:LamTaylor}
		\Lambda_t(k)=\int_\mu^k (k-x)\,\Lambda_t''(x)\,dx.
	\end{align}
	For $x\in[\mu,k]$, the four curvature terms satisfy
	\begin{align*}
		\frac1x     & \leqslant\frac1\mu,
		            & \frac1{m-x}           & \leqslant\frac1{m-k},        \\
		\frac1{t-x} & \leqslant\frac2{(n-1)\mu},
		            & \frac1{N-m-t+x}       & \leqslant\frac1{(n-1)(m-k)}.
	\end{align*}
	For the third bound, use $t-k=(n-1)\mu-(k-\mu)\geqslant(n-1)\mu/2$.
	For the fourth, use $x\geqslant\mu$ and $m-\mu\geqslant m-k$.
	Insert these bounds in~\eqref{eq:LamTaylor}.
	Since $\int_\mu^k(k-x)\,dx=(k-\mu)^2/2$, we obtain
	\[
		\Lambda_t(k)\leqslant \frac{(k-\mu)^2}{2}\biggl(1+\frac{2}{n-1}\biggr)\biggl(\frac1\mu+\frac1{m-k}\biggr)\leqslant (k-\mu)^2\biggl(\frac1\mu+\frac1{m-k}\biggr)
	\]
	for $n\geqslant3$, which is~\eqref{eq:LamF1}.
	For~\eqref{eq:LamF2}, treat the terms $1/(m-x)$ and $1/(N-m-t+x)$ separately.	We have
    \begin{align*}
	   \int_\mu^k\frac{k-x}{m-x}dx &\leqslant k-\mu\text{ as } \frac{k-x}{m-x}\leqslant1,\text{ and }\\ 
       \int_\mu^k\frac{k-x}{N-m-t+x}dx&\leqslant \frac{(k-\mu)^2}{2(n-1)(m-\mu)}\leqslant\frac{k-\mu}{2(n-1)}\text{ as }k-\mu\leqslant m-\mu.
    \end{align*}
    Hence
	\[
		\Lambda_t(k)\leqslant \frac{(k-\mu)^2}{2}\biggl(\frac1\mu+\frac{2}{(n-1)\mu}\biggr)+(k-\mu)\biggl(1+\frac{1}{2(n-1)}\biggr)\leqslant \frac{(k-\mu)^2}{\mu}+2(k-\mu)
	\]
	for $n\geqslant 3$.

label: lem:tjlocG
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:tjlocG}
	There is an absolute constant $n_0$ such that for all $n\geqslant n_0$, $m\geqslant1$ and $2\log n\leqslant j\leqslant m-1$,
	\[
		t_j\leqslant n\,(j-D_j),\text{ \emph{i.e.,}\ } d_j:=j-{t_j}/{n}\ \geqslant\ D_j.
	\]
head: environment
name: Location of $t_j$, Gaussian regime

label: eq:blocksum
title: Proof
body_md:
Define $t=\lfloor n(j-D_j)\rfloor$, $\mu=t/n$ and $d=j-\mu$.
	Then $D_j\leqslant d\leqslant D_j+1/n$.
	We will show that $$
    np_j(t)\geqslant1.
    $$
	Since $D_j\leqslant j/6$, we have $\mu\geqslant5j/6-1/n\geqslant j/2$.
	The ratio estimates in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:hyp}.\ref{hyp:c} show that $h_t$ is nonincreasing above $j$.
	Hence, for every integer $b\geqslant1$ with $j+b-1\leqslant m-1$,
	\begin{align}\label{eq:blocksum}
		p_j(t)\ \geqslant\ \sum_{i=j}^{j+b-1}h_t(i)\ \geqslant\ b\,h_t(k),\quad k:=j+b-1.
	\end{align}

	We will apply Lemma~\ref{lem:stirling} to $h_t(k)$.
	Each block chosen below has $j\leqslant k\leqslant\min(2j-1,m-1)$.
	For $n\geqslant9$, its hypotheses follow from
	\begin{align*}
		t-k   & \geqslant n\mu-2j\geqslant(n/2-2)j\geqslant1, \\
		t-k   & \leqslant(n-1)j-nD_j\leqslant(n-1)m-1,   \\
		k-\mu & \leqslant2j\leqslant4\mu\leqslant(n-1)\mu/2.
	\end{align*}
	Here $m-j\geqslant1$ and $\mu\geqslant j/2$.
	Since $j\geqslant2\log n$, we can assume $j\geqslant200$ by increasing $n_0$.


	\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Case 1: $m\geqslant 3j$.} Take $b:=\lceil\sqrt j\rceil$, so $k\leqslant 2j-1\leqslant m-1$ and $m-k\geqslant m-2j\geqslant j\geqslant \mu$. By~\eqref{eq:hstirling}, $\frac{b}{7\sqrt{k(1-k/m)}}\geqslant \frac{\sqrt j}{7\sqrt{2j}}\geqslant \frac1{10}$, hence $p_j(t)\geqslant \frac1{10}e^{-\Lambda_t(k)}$. By~\eqref{eq:LamF1} and $m-k\geqslant\mu\geqslant j/2$,
	\[
		\Lambda_t(k)\leqslant \frac{2(k-\mu)^2}{\mu}\leqslant \frac{4(k-\mu)^2}{j},\quad k-\mu=d+b-1\leqslant \frac16\sqrt{j\log n}+\sqrt j+2\leqslant \frac14\sqrt{j\log n}
	\]
	for $n\geqslant n_0$ (as $\sqrt j+2\leqslant \frac{1}{12}\sqrt{j\log n}$ once $\log n\geqslant 144(1+2/\sqrt{200})^2$). Thus $\Lambda_t(k)\leqslant \frac14\log n$ and $np_j(t)\geqslant \frac{n^{3/4}}{10}\geqslant1$.

	\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Case 2: $m<3j$ and $m-j\geqslant 225$.} Take $b:=\lceil\sqrt{m-j}\rceil\leqslant \frac{m-j}{2}$, so $k\leqslant m-1$ and $m-k\geqslant (m-j)/{2}$. Since $k(1-k/m)\leqslant m-k\leqslant m-j$, $\frac{b}{7\sqrt{k(1-k/m)}}\geqslant\frac17$. Hence $p_j(t)\geqslant\frac17 e^{-\Lambda_t(k)}$. Now $m-j<2j\leqslant 4\mu$, so $\frac1\mu\leqslant\frac{4}{m-j}$, and~\eqref{eq:LamF1} gives
	\[
		\Lambda_t(k)\leqslant (k-\mu)^2\biggl(\frac{4}{m-j}+\frac{2}{m-j}\biggr)=\frac{6(k-\mu)^2}{m-j},
	\]
	where
	\[
		k-\mu\leqslant \frac16\sqrt{(m-j)\log n}+\sqrt{m-j}+2\leqslant \sqrt{m-j}\biggl(\frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{6}+\frac{17}{15}\biggr),
	\]
	using $2\leqslant \frac{2}{15}\sqrt{m-j}$. In particular, $\Lambda_t(k)\leqslant 6\Bigl(\frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{6}+\frac{17}{15}\Bigr)^2\leqslant \log n-\log 7$ for $n\geqslant n_0$, and $np_j(t)\geqslant1$.

	\smallskip\noindent\textbf{Case 3: $m-j\leqslant 224$.} Take $b=1$, $k=j$. Then $k(1-k/m)\leqslant m-j\leqslant 224$, so~\eqref{eq:hstirling} gives $p_j(t)\geqslant h_t(j)\geqslant \frac{1}{105}e^{-\Lambda_t(j)}$. Here $d\leqslant \frac14\log n+\frac1n$ and $\mu=j-d\geqslant 2\log n-\frac14\log n-1\geqslant \frac32\log n$, so~\eqref{eq:LamF2} gives
	\[
		\Lambda_t(j)\leqslant \frac{d^2}{\mu}+2d\leqslant \frac{(\frac14\log n+1)^2}{\frac32\log n}+\frac12\log n+2\leqslant \frac{3}{5}\log n\leqslant \log n-\log 105
	\]
	for $n\geqslant n_0$, and again $np_j(t)\geqslant1$.

label: lem:elastG
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first inequality in~\eqref{eq:phiG} was shown in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:elastj} (it only needs $r_j(s)<1$, which holds for $s\leqslant nj$). From~\eqref{eq:ratio}, with $s=n\mu$ and $N=nm$, a direct expansion gives
	\[
		1-r_j(s)=\frac{(j+1)(N-m-s+j+1)-(m-j)(s-j)}{(j+1)(N-m-s+j+1)}
		=\frac{nm(d+1)-n\mu-m+2j+1}{(j+1)\bigl(n(m-\mu)-(m-j-1)\bigr)}.
	\]
	The numerator is at least $nmd-m+n(m-\mu)\geqslant nmd-m$ (as $\mu\leqslant j\leqslant m$), and the denominator is at most $(j+1)n(m-\mu)$ because $m-j-1\geqslant0$. For $d\geqslant1/n$, these comparisons give the second inequality in~\eqref{eq:phiG}.
	If $d<1/n$, its right-hand side is negative whereas $1-r_j(s)>0$, so the inequality also holds.

	The function $d\mapsto m(d-1/n)/(m-j+d)$ is nondecreasing.
	In the stated window, $d\geqslant D_j/2$.
	Together with $j/(j+1)\geqslant1/2$, this proves $j\phi_j(s)\geqslant\beta_j$.

	For the upper bounds, first note $\beta_j\leqslant m/2$.
	If $j\geqslant m/2$, then $\beta_j\leqslant j\leqslant t_j$.
	If $j<m/2$, then $m-j+D_j/2>m/2$ and $\beta_j<D_j/2\leqslant j\leqslant t_j$.
	In either case, $\beta_j\leqslant3j/2$.

	For the lower bound, use the three cases in~\eqref{eq:Dj}.
	For sufficiently large $n$, each gives $D_j\geqslant(5/2)\sqrt{\log n}$.
	In the middle case, this follows from $m-j\geqslant225$.
	Thus $D_j/2-1/n\geqslant2D_j/5$ after increasing $n_0$.
    \begin{enumerate}[label={Case~\arabic*.},leftmargin=5em]
        \item ($m\geqslant3j$): $m-j+D_j/2\leqslant m$, so $\beta_j\geqslant \frac{D_j/2-1/n}{2}\geqslant \frac{D_j}{5}=\frac{\sqrt{j\log n}}{30}$.

    	\item ($m<3j$, $m-j\geqslant225$):
	If $D_j/2\geqslant m-j$, then
	\[
		\beta_j\geqslant\frac{m(D_j/2-1/n)}{2D_j}\geqslant\frac m5.
	\]
	Otherwise,
	\[
		\beta_j\geqslant\frac{m(D_j/2-1/n)}{4(m-j)}
		\geqslant\frac{mD_j}{10(m-j)}
		=\frac m{60}\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{m-j}}
		\geqslant\frac{\sqrt{m\log n}}{60}.
	\]
	Both bounds imply $\beta_j\geqslant\sqrt{j\log n}/60$.
	Here $m\geqslant j\geqslant2\log n$.

    	\item ($m-j\leqslant 224$): for $n\geqslant n_0$ we have $D_j/2=\frac18\log n\geqslant 224\geqslant m-j$, so as in the first sub-case of Case 2, $\beta_j\geqslant \frac m5\geqslant\frac15\sqrt{j\log n}$.
    \end{enumerate}

	Finally, Lemma~\ref{lem:hyp}\ref{hyp:b} gives
	\[
		\frac{p_j(t)}{p_j(t+1)}
		=1-\frac{j\phi_j(t+1)}{t+1}
		\leqslant\exp\left(-\frac{\beta_j}{t+1}\right)
	\]
	for $j-1\leqslant t\leqslant n(j-D_j/2)-1$.
	Iteration proves~\eqref{eq:elastG}.

label: prop:logTjG
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:logTjG}
	There exist absolute constants $C$ and $n_0$ such that for all $n\geqslant n_0$, $m\geqslant 1$ and $2\log n\leqslant j\leqslant m-1$,
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{E}}\bigl(\log^2(\tau_j/t_j)\bigr)\leqslant \frac{C}{j\log n}.
	\]
	Moreover, for all $n\geqslant2$ and $m\geqslant1$, $\operatorname{\mathds{E}}\bigl(\log^2(\tau_m/t_m)\bigr)\leqslant C/m^2$.
head: environment

label: eq:betaxstar
title: Proof
body_md:
We follow the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:logTjlog}, with $\beta:=\beta_j$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:elastG}, $\alpha:=\sqrt j/e^2$, $g(t)=np_j(t)$, and the window end
	\[
		E:=\lfloor n(j-D_j/2)\rfloor,\quad x_*:=\log\frac{E}{t_j}.
	\]
	By Lemma~\ref{lem:tjlocG}, $t_j\leqslant n(j-D_j)$, hence
	\[
		\frac{E}{t_j}\geqslant \frac{j-D_j/2-1/n}{j-D_j}=1+\frac{D_j/2-1/n}{j-D_j}\geqslant 1+\frac{D_j}{3j},\quad x_*\geqslant \log\biggl(1+\frac{D_j}{3j}\biggr)\geqslant \frac{D_j}{6j},
	\]
	using $D_j\leqslant j$ and $\log(1+y)\geqslant y/2$ for $y\in[0,1]$.
	The lower bounds for $\beta$ give explicit window products.
	In Case 1, $\beta x_*\geqslant(\log n)/1080$.
	In Case 2 with $D_j/2\geqslant m-j$, the product is at least $D_j/30\geqslant\sqrt{\log n}/12$.
	In the other subcase, it is at least $D_j^2/\{60(m-j)\}=(\log n)/2160$.
	In Case 3, it is at least $D_j/30=(\log n)/120$.
	Hence
	\begin{align}\label{eq:betaxstar}
		\beta x_*\ \geqslant\ \kappa_n:=\min\left\{\frac{\log n}{2160},\ \frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{12}\right\}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\infty.
	\end{align}

	For $n\geqslant n_0$,~\eqref{eq:betaxstar} ensures $\beta x_*\geqslant6$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:tailwindow} with $U=\tau_j$, $h=t_j$, $R=nj$, and the elasticities~\eqref{eq:elastG} and~\eqref{eq:elast}.
	Its hypotheses follow from $\beta\leqslant t_j$ and $\alpha\leqslant E$. Hence
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{E}}\log^2(\tau_j/t_j)\leqslant
		C\left(\frac1{\beta^2}+\frac{e^{-K}}{\alpha^2}
		+\frac{e^{-K/2}}{\alpha\beta}\right),\quad K\geqslant e^{\kappa_n/2}.
	\]
	By~\eqref{eq:betaG}, $\beta^2\geqslant j\log n/3600$. Also $\alpha^2=j/e^4$ and, for sufficiently large $n$, $\beta\geqslant\sqrt j$. Since $e^{-K/2}\leqslant1/\log n$ for large $n$, all three terms are bounded by $C/(j\log n)$.

	For $j=m$, $p_m(t)=h_t(m)$ and $\phi_m(s)=1$. Lemma~\ref{lem:hyp}\ref{hyp:b} yields
	\[
		\frac{p_m(t)}{p_m(t+1)}=1-\frac m{t+1}\leqslant e^{-m/(t+1)}
	\]
	for $m-1\leqslant t\leqslant N-1$. Thus the full-window elasticity has exponent $m$ up to $N$. The first part of Lemma~\ref{lem:tailwindow}, with $h=t_m$, $E=R=N$ and $\beta=m\leqslant t_m$, proves $\operatorname{\mathds{E}}\log^2(\tau_m/t_m)\leqslant C/m^2$.

label: cor:fixedmS
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:fixedmS}
	Fix $m\geqslant1$.
	Let $E_2,\ldots,E_m$ be independent exponential random variables of mean one.
	Then, as $n\to\infty$,
	\[
		S_{n,m}-\operatorname{\mathds{E}} S_{n,m}
		\implies-\sum_{j=2}^{m}\frac{\log E_j+\gamma}{j},
		\quad
		\operatorname{Var}(S_{n,m})\to\frac{\pi^2}{6}\sum_{j=2}^{m}\frac1{j^2}.
	\]
	Both sums are zero when $m=1$.
head: environment
name: Compensator limit for fixed multiplicity

title: Proof
body_md:
For $m=1$, $W_t=1$ for $t\geqslant1$ and $S_{n,1}=\mathcal{H}_n$.
	Now suppose $m\geqslant2$.
	Set $b_j=(j!n^{j-1}/\kappa_{m,j})^{1/j}$.
	He and Ottolini~\cite[Theorem 4.1]{He_2023} prove a joint Poisson approximation for the birthday counts.
	Their last time without a $j$-fold repeat is $\tau_j-1$ in our notation.
	At $t_j'=\lfloor b_j y_j^{1/j}\rfloor$, their Poisson parameter tends to $y_j$.
	For fixed positive $y_2,\ldots,y_m$, the times are eventually ordered because their powers of $n$ strictly increase.
	Their joint survival estimate therefore gives
	\[
		\operatorname{\mathds{P}}(\tau_j>t_j'\text{ for all }2\leqslant j\leqslant m)
		\longrightarrow\exp\left(-\sum_{j=2}^{m}y_j\right).
	\]
	Applying the same result to subsets of indices gives the joint distributional limit
	\[
		\left((\tau_j/b_j)^j\right)_{j=2}^{m}
		\implies(E_j)_{j=2}^{m}.
	\]
	The full-window bounds in Lemma~\ref{lem:tailwindow} give bounded fourth moments of $\log(\tau_j/b_j)$.
	Thus the logarithms and their pairwise products are uniformly integrable.
	The first two joint moments consequently converge.
	The harmonic-number error tends to zero in $L^2$, since it is bounded by $C/\tau_j$ and $\tau_j\to\infty$ in probability.
	Use~\eqref{eq:STj} and center each term.
	The joint limit yields the displayed law, and independence gives the variance constant.

title: Remark
body_md:
The expansion~\eqref{eq:logTjasymp} recovers the fixed-$m$ mean asymptotics of~\cite{He_2023}.
	For $j\geqslant2$, $\tau_j\to\infty$ in probability.
	The deterministic error in $\mathcal{H}_{a-1}=\log a+\gamma+O(1/a)$ is bounded for $a\geqslant1$.
	Hence $\operatorname{\mathds{E}}\mathcal{H}_{\tau_j-1}=\operatorname{\mathds{E}}\log\tau_j+\gamma+o(1)$ since the error is uniformly bounded and tends to zero in probability.
	The level $j=1$ contributes $\mathcal{H}_0=0$.
	Inserting~\eqref{eq:logTjasymp} in the representation~\eqref{eq:STj} and using $\mathcal{H}_N=\log n+\log m+\gamma+o(1)$ gives
	\begin{align*}
		\operatorname{\mathds{E}} S_{n,m} & =m\,\mathcal{H}_N-\sum_{j=2}^m\bigl(\operatorname{\mathds{E}}(\log \tau_j)+\gamma\bigr)+o(1)
		=\mathcal{H}_m(\log n+\gamma)+\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\frac1j\log\binom mj+o(1),
	\end{align*}
	which agrees with $\mathcal{H}_m\mathcal{H}_n+\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\frac1j\log\binom mj$ up to $o(1)$.

label: rem:fixednSDE
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:fixednSDE}
	The bridge functional admits a diffusion description.
	This gives a stochastic representation of its distribution.
	Define
	\[
		P_n=I_n-n^{-1}\boldsymbol1\boldsymbol1^{\mathsf T},\quad
		\mathsf H_n=\{x\in\mathds{R}^n:\sum x_i=0\},\quad g(x)=\max_i x_i.
	\]
	For standard $n$-dimensional Brownian motion $\boldsymbol{W}$, consider
	\begin{align}\label{eq:bridgeSDE}
		dX(u)& =P_nd\boldsymbol{W}(u)-\frac{X(u)}{1-u}\,du,
		      \ X(0) =0,\quad\text{ and }\quad
		dA(u) =\frac{g(X(u))}{u}\,du,
		      \  A(0)=0.
	\end{align}
	The linear SDE has the unique solution
	$
		X(u)=(1-u)\int_0^u {P_n d\boldsymbol{W}(v)}/(1-v).
	$
	Its covariance is $(\min(u,v)-uv)P_n$.
	Thus $X$ has the law of $(B_i-\overline B)_{i\leqslant n}$ and extends continuously to $X(1)=0$.
	The endpoint estimates above make the improper integral for $A$ well defined in $L^2$.
	Hence $\mathcal{B}_n\stackrel d=A(1)$.
head: environment
name: SDE representations
